cards.text: The LORD has just given the priests and Levites their duties. Now He speaks to Moses and Aaron again. Moses is Israel's leader and Aaron is his brother, the priest, and this new statute starts with the Israelites bringing them an animal.

cards.question: What animal are the Israelites told to bring to Moses and Aaron?

answers.text: A red heifer with no defect
A male goat from the flock

cards.text: This heifer has also never been placed under a yoke, so she's never worked a single day. I've been on the job since Mother Miller paid a quarter for me, and I'm a LITTLE jealous.

cards.question: Moses and Aaron are told to hand the red heifer over to a priest from Aaron's family. Which priest?
True or false: the red heifer is slaughtered at the altar in front of the Tent of Meeting.

cards.text: Eleazar is Aaron's son. The heifer is slaughtered outside the camp while he watches, and then he takes some of its blood on his finger.

cards.question: Eleazar sprinkles the heifer's blood ___ times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting.

cards.text: Then the heifer is burned while Eleazar watches: hide, flesh, blood, even the dung. Friend, I've burned plenty of batches, but NEVER on purpose.

cards.question: The priest throws three things onto the burning heifer: cedar wood, ___ and scarlet ___.

cards.text: Next the priest washes his clothes, bathes his body in water and goes back into the camp. The man who burned the heifer has to wash and bathe too.

cards.question: After washing, how long do the priest and the man who burned the heifer stay ceremonially unclean?

cards.text: Then a man who is ceremonially clean gathers up the ashes and stores them in a clean place outside the camp. Israel holds on to those ashes the way I hold on to my last bag of chocolate chips.

cards.question: The congregation keeps the heifer's ashes for preparing the water of ___.
The man who gathered up the ashes was ceremonially clean. True or false: he stays clean and doesn't have to wash anything.

cards.text: So he washes his clothes and stays unclean until evening, just like the other two. That's three men doing laundry over one heifer, and friend, I'm a stamper, I've never washed a THING.

cards.question: The LORD calls this a permanent statute. Who is it for?

answers.text: The Israelites and foreigners living among them
Only the priests from Aaron's family
Only the Levites who serve the Tent

cards.text: Now the statute turns to the people who will need those ashes. Whoever touches any dead body becomes unclean.

cards.question: Whoever touches any dead body is unclean for ___ days.

cards.text: To be clean again, that person has to purify himself with the water. Not once, friend. TWICE.

cards.question: On which days does the unclean person purify himself with the water?
Someone touches a human corpse and never purifies himself. True or false: he defiles the tabernacle of the LORD.

cards.text: That person must be cut off from Israel, and his uncleanness is still on him. Next, when someone dies in a tent, everyone who enters and everyone already inside is unclean for seven days.

cards.question: When someone dies in a tent, true or false: an open container in there without a lid fastened on it is unclean too.

cards.text: Note to self: lid on the sprinkles, EVERY night. Out in the open field, touching someone who was killed by the sword or died of natural causes also means seven days unclean.

cards.question: Out in the open field, what else besides a body makes someone unclean for seven days?

answers.text: Touching a human bone or a grave
Touching a soldier's sword or shield
Hearing news of a death in battle

cards.text: So here's where those stored-up ashes come in. Some of the ashes of the burnt sin offering go into a jar.

cards.question: The ashes go into a jar, and ___ water is poured over them.

cards.text: Then a man who is ceremonially clean takes some hyssop and dips it in the water.

cards.question: When someone has died in a tent, what does the clean man sprinkle with the hyssop?

answers.text: The tent and its furnishings and the people
Only the body and the bed it lay on
Only the doorway and the tent pegs

cards.question: The clean man also sprinkles anyone who touched a bone or a grave or a dead body, on the third day and the seventh day. True or false: right after the seventh day's sprinkling, that person is clean.

cards.text: First he washes his clothes and bathes in water, and that evening he's clean. But if he skips it, he's cut off from the assembly, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD.

cards.question: Here's a twist about the clean man who sprinkles the water of purification. What does he have to do?

answers.text: He stays holy for seven days
He is clean for a full year

cards.text: And whoever touches the water of purification is unclean until evening. So the man getting everybody clean has some cleaning up of his own to do, like scrubbing the whole kitchen and ending up the messiest thing in it.

cards.question: One last rule: anything the unclean person touches becomes ___.

cards.text: And anyone who touches that thing is unclean until evening. From one red heifer to one jar of water, friend, God has given His people a way to be made clean again.

findings.problem: The opening card states facts from outside the passage with no reference. It says the LORD has just given the priests and Levites their duties (Numbers 18) and that Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). The card cites only Numbers 19:1-2.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The joke "I've been on the job since Mother Miller paid a quarter for me" adds something new to his backstory and contradicts it. He spent years unused in the junk drawer, so he has not been on the job the whole time since the Millers bought him.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The question says Eleazar is 'a priest from Aaron's family.' Numbers 19 never says this, and the card gives no reference for it. The card cites only Numbers 19:3.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The card says 'Eleazar is Aaron's son.' This fact comes from outside the passage (Exodus 6:23; Numbers 3:2), but the card cites only Numbers 19:3-4.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The two-blank card asks the baker to fill in 'hyssop' and 'wool' from the list of items in verse 6. Nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason these out. It is a guess at wording the baker hasn't seen.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The blank 'fresh' water is a single word from verse 17. The baker can't reason it out from the earlier cards, so it tests wording, not meaning.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: 'But if he skips it' follows the sentence about washing clothes and bathing, so 'it' reads as the washing. Verse 20 says the person is cut off if he 'does not purify himself,' meaning the sprinkling. The card should say that.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Calling it 'a twist' rules out the two wrong answers, which are both pleasant outcomes ('stays holy,' 'clean for a full year'). The wrong answers also aren't things he 'has to do,' so they aren't the same kind of answer as the right one. The right answer stands out.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The whole of Numbers 19 is ritual law: how the ashes are made, then rules for uncleanness from the dead. The long-stretch rule says rules for offerings and everyday life get one summary story card and no choice cards. Applied strictly, that would leave almost nothing to ask. The walkthrough treated it as key law instead. The passage is also typed Narrative, though it contains no events.
findings.question: When an entire passage is ritual or everyday-life law, should the long-stretch rule apply? Or should the passage be treated like key law, with full story cards and choice cards, as done here?
